newsitem.title: USA: U.S. faulted over downing of planes by Cuba. [CORRECTED 22:15 GMT]
newsitem.headline: U.S. faulted over downing of planes by Cuba. [CORRECTED 22:15 GMT]

text.p: The president of an anti-Castro group said on Wednesday the U.S. military failed to warn the pilots of two private planes that they were in danger before they were shot down by Cuban Migs last February.
The two small planes operated by Brothers to the Rescue were downed last Feb. 24, killing all four men onboard. They were looking for Cubans trying to reach the United States by boat.
Cuba said the planes were in its airspace. The United States said they were over international waters and condemned Cuba for shooting down civilian aircraft.

Jose Basulto of Brothers to the Rescue said at a congressional hearing the U.S. Air Force saw on radar that the Migs were heading for the aircraft but failed to alert the pilots or send up U.S. fighters from bases in Florida to protect them.

"Expert witnesses have confirmed that U.S. government authorities at a minimum, wilfully chose not to act to protect the lives and planes on that fateful mission," Basulto told the House Western Hemisphere subcommittee.
Basulto was piloting a third plane that was chased back to U.S. airspace by the Migs.
Representative Ileana Ros-Lehtinen, a Florida Republican (corrects party affiliation frrom Democrat) and a Cuban American, also questioned the actions of the Air Force.
"Why did the Air Force not inform Brothers to the Rescue of the presence of Cuban Migs even after they knew that the Brother's flight plan would take them close to them?

"Why was no action taken to intercept the Cuban Migs pursuing Brothers to the Rescue aircraft before two of the planes were shot down?" she asked. But Ros-Lehtinen said Fidel Castro was responsible for the deaths.
Deputy Assistant Defence Secretary Maria Fernandez, herself a Cuban-American, also blamed Cuba and said the U.S. military had acted properly.

"There is no justification for the Cuban government's use of deadly force against civilian aircraft. We were not in a position to anticipate the Cuban government's downing of the aircraft," Fernandez said.

Howard DeWolf, director of the Defence Department's Inter-American Region, said in a letter to Ros-Lehtinen that Basulto had been warned several times about the dangers of flying in or near Cuban airspace.
DeWolf said Cuban aircraft did not approach the southern boundary of the U.S. air defence zone during the incident. He said U.S. aircraft would have intercepted them if they had.
